name: Hudle
tagline: App for finding and booking sports venues, badminton courts, turfs, pools, plus joining open games with strangers in Indian cities.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Revenue is mostly per-booking plus a paid pass tier, not a flat monthly SaaS fee.

verdictSummary: Hudle is not software you pay for, it is a two-sided marketplace: on one side thousands of turf and court owners with live slot inventory, on the other people who want to play badminton at 7pm tonight. An agent can absolutely build you a booking UI in an afternoon. It cannot build you the venues, their calendars, their willingness to honour your reservation, or the strangers who show up to fill your football game. What you would be cloning is the thin part. The useful part is a sales team that signed up venue operators city by city and a user base dense enough that open games actually fill.
coreLoopDIY: A private web app where you track your regular venues, their prices and slot times, log bookings your group has actually made by phone, and split the bill.
requirements: Node and SQLite locally, or a cheap VPS if your group needs shared access
You still call or WhatsApp the venue yourself to confirm a slot
A list of venues you already know, since there is no inventory feed to pull from
whatYouLose: Live slot availability across hundreds of venues you have never heard of
Actual booking confirmation, your DIY app just records intentions
Open games and pickup matches with people outside your contact list
Payments, refunds and the venue honouring a digital booking without argument
Discovery when you travel to another city
moatNotes: Venue inventory in Indian metros was assembled on foot, venue by venue. That is not scrapeable and it is not one-shottable.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is a WhatsApp group, six phone calls and a turf owner who says the slot is free and then double books it. Hudle collapses that into a tap, and if your regular four is only three, open games find you a fourth. The pass tiers are a discount mechanic on top of that convenience, not a software subscription. None of that value lives in the app code.
notes: The booking screen is an afternoon; the venues are years of field sales. The moat is signed-up turf owners with live inventory plus enough players nearby that an open game actually fills.
prompt:
Build a local-first web app called "CourtLog" for tracking a small group's recurring sports bookings. Do not try to be a marketplace.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/courtlog.db, schema created on first run.
- No auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no external APIs. Single trusted user or a small group on a LAN.
- Any secrets go in .env, read with process.env, and .env is gitignored. There should be none.

Data model:
- venue: name, sport, address, phone, maps_url, hourly_price_paise, notes.
- slot: venue_id, weekday, start_time, end_time, typical_availability note.
- booking: venue_id, date, start_time, end_time, total_paise, status (planned | confirmed | played | cancelled), notes.
- player: name, phone.
- booking_player: booking_id, player_id, share_paise, paid boolean.

Screens:
1. Venues list and detail with an editable set of usual slots and a "call venue" tel: link.
2. New booking form: pick venue, date, time, auto-fill total from hourly price, tick which players are in, split the total evenly with manual override.
3. Upcoming view grouped by date, plus a past view.
4. Balances page: per player, total owed and total paid, with a one-tap mark-paid.
5. Export everything to JSON from a button.

Explicitly out of scope: real availability, online payment, push notifications, finding venues you do not already know, matching with strangers.

Seed the db with two fake venues and four players so the UI is not empty. Include a README with run instructions and one paragraph stating plainly that this app does not book anything, you still have to phone the venue.
